blocks.prompt: The Wheel That Makes You Strong
blocks.text:
A pulley is a wheel with a groove cut around the edge. A rope rides in that groove. When you pull the rope one way, the load moves the other way. That is the whole idea. Pull down, and the load goes up.

Sailors put pulleys all over their ships to raise the sails. Builders hang pulleys from cranes. There is a pulley at the top of every flagpole, and one hidden inside your window blind. Even an elevator hangs from thick ropes that run over a big pulley.

A pulley does not make the load lighter. It just lets you pull in an easier direction.

3.title: The Wheel That Makes You Strong

blocks.prompt: Pull Down, Lift Up
blocks.text:
A pulley is one of the simple machines, and it is the easiest one to spot. Look for a wheel with a groove around its rim and a rope sitting in the groove.

The simplest kind is a fixed pulley. It is bolted in place, like the one at the top of a flagpole. You pull the rope down and the flag goes up. The pulley does not make the flag lighter. It only changes the direction of your pull, and pulling down is much easier than pushing up, because you can lean your whole weight into it.

The clever kind is a movable pulley. This one is not bolted anywhere. It hangs on the rope and rides up with the load. Now two lengths of rope share the weight instead of one, so you only pull half as hard. There is a catch. To lift the load one step, you have to pull two steps of rope. You save force and you spend distance.

Hook several pulleys together and you get a block and tackle. Count the ropes holding the load. That is how many times you divide the force you need.

Its housing is called a block
Fixed pulley: direction only, no force saved
Movable pulley: half the force, twice the rope

blocks.prompt: The Trade You Make
blocks.text:
Give a kid a rope and a heavy box and they will figure out fast that lifting straight up is miserable. Your arms are weak at that angle, and there is nowhere to put your body weight. Now hang a wheel from a beam, drape the rope over it, and the same job feels different. You pull down instead of up. You can hang off the rope. The box rises. Nothing about the box changed. The direction of your effort did. That is a fixed pulley, and it is the plainest trick in engineering.

The movable pulley is a better trick. Attach the pulley to the box itself and tie one end of the rope to the beam above. Run the rope down through the pulley and back up. Now the box hangs from two strands of rope, and each strand carries half the weight. You pull with half the force. But physics keeps its books carefully. To raise the box one foot, both strands must shorten by one foot, so you haul two feet of rope through your hands. You bought force with distance.

Combine fixed and movable pulleys into a frame and you have a block and tackle. Sailors used them everywhere, because a wooden warship's sails weighed more than a crew could lift bare handed. The rule is simple enough to use on the spot: count the rope strands actually supporting the load. Four strands means you pull with roughly a quarter of the force and roughly four times the rope. Roughly, because rope stiffness and friction in the wheels always steal a little back.

blocks.prompt: No Free Lunch, But a Very Good Deal
blocks.text:
A pulley is a wheel with a groove around its rim and a rope running in the groove. That is the entire machine. There are no gears, no motor, and nothing to break except the rope. It is also one of the six simple machines that ancient engineers had to work with, and it is arguably the most useful of them.

Start with a fixed pulley, the kind at the top of a flagpole. The wheel is bolted to the pole and goes nowhere. Pull down, and the flag climbs. This buys you no strength at all. A twenty pound flag still takes twenty pounds of pull. What it buys you is direction, and direction is worth more than it sounds. Pulling down lets you add your own body weight to the job. Pushing up lets you add nothing.

The movable pulley is where the real bargain begins. Fasten the wheel to the load, anchor one end of the rope overhead, and run the free end down around the wheel and back up. The load now hangs from two strands, each holding half. You pull half as hard. In exchange, you pull twice as far, because both strands have to shorten for the load to rise at all.

That exchange is not a coincidence and it is not negotiable. Force multiplied by distance is work, and a machine cannot create work out of nothing. It can only reshape it, spreading a large force over a short distance into a small force over a long one. Every simple machine makes the same bargain in its own accent.

You can find the same bargain in an elevator shaft, though it hides. The car hangs from cables that run over a grooved wheel at the top of the building, and on the other side of that wheel hangs a counterweight, heavy enough to balance the car and part of a full load. The motor is not lifting the car. It is nudging the small difference between two nearly equal weights, which is why an elevator motor is far smaller than the load it appears to be lifting.

Stack several wheels into a block and tackle and the bargain scales. Count the strands supporting the load: six strands, one sixth the force, six times the rope. Ancient writers tell a story about Archimedes using such a rig to haul a loaded ship out of the water by himself, to prove a point to a king. The story may be polished. The physics is not.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Sheave: the grooved wheel. Block: its housing
Mechanical advantage equals supporting strands
Work is conserved: force times distance
Roman treadwheel cranes used compound tackle
Portsmouth Block Mills, around 1803
Often called the first mass production line

blocks.prompt: Give Me a Place to Stand
blocks.text:
Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth. Archimedes probably never said it in those words, but the boast has stuck to him for twenty two centuries because it captures something true about simple machines: with the right arrangement of wheels and rope, there is no upper limit to what a single person can lift. There is only a limit to how long they are willing to pull.

Start with the machine itself, which is almost insultingly plain. A pulley is a grooved wheel, called a sheave, mounted in a housing, called a block, with a rope riding in the groove. No gears. No power source. Nothing to calibrate.

A fixed pulley, bolted to a beam, gives you nothing but direction. Twenty pounds of load still demands twenty pounds of pull. That sounds like a swindle until you notice that a human body is built to pull down, not to push up: you can hang your entire weight from a downward rope and contribute nothing but arm strength to an upward one. Redirecting a force is not the same as reducing it, but it is not nothing.

The movable pulley reduces it. Anchor the rope overhead, pass it down under a wheel fixed to the load, and haul the free end back up. The load now hangs from two strands, each carrying half its weight, and your pull is halved. The universe then presents the invoice. To lift the load one foot, each of the two strands must shorten one foot, so two feet of rope must pass through your hands. Force down, distance up, product unchanged. That product, force multiplied by distance, is work, and no machine has ever manufactured any. A pulley system is not a source of effort. It is a currency exchange, and it charges a small commission in friction and rope stiffness on every transaction.

Combine the two kinds into a block and tackle and the exchange rate is yours to set. Count the strands that actually support the load: five strands, one fifth the force, five times the rope. This is why Roman crews with a compound tackle and a treadwheel could set stone blocks weighing several tons, and why every wooden warship was strung with hundreds of blocks. A ship of the line carried well over a thousand of them, each one shaped by hand.

That last fact turned out to matter more than the ships did. Around 1803, at Portsmouth, Marc Brunel and Henry Maudslay built a set of machines to make navy blocks by steps: sawing, boring, shaping, each machine doing one task perfectly and passing the piece along. Ten unskilled men, the accounts say, replaced the output of one hundred and ten skilled blockmakers. Historians generally count it as the first mass production line in the world. The humble pulley, the machine that makes strength out of patience, quietly taught the factory how to think.

You still live inside the bargain. The elevator you ride hangs from cables over a sheave, balanced by a counterweight on the far side, so the motor only argues with the difference. Your window blind, the crane on the skyline, the gym machine with the stack of plates, the sail of a boat: all of them are wheels with rope in the groove, trading your distance for their force, exactly as they did for Archimedes.
